front.title: Clarifying Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) Segment Identifier (SID) List Processing

abstract.t: Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) is the instantiation of Segment Routing (SR) on the IPv6 data plane. Segments are indicated by Segment Identifiers (SIDs). SRv6 utilizes the Segment Routing Header (SRH), an IPv6 extension header that includes a SID list indicating the sequence of segments and any additional processing to be performed.
This document updates RFC 8754 by clarifying the processing of SID list entries. It does not change any elements of the SRv6 architecture.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The Segment Routing (SR) architecture is specified in . SR forwards packets along a series of segments, and it may perform additional segment-specific processing on packets. Segments are indicated by Segment Identifiers (SIDs).

The mechanisms to achieve Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) include the use of the Segment Routing Header (SRH) , an IPv6 extension header that includes a SID list indicating the sequence of segments and any additional processing to be performed.
This document updates by clarifying the processing of SID list entries. It does not change any elements of the SRv6 architecture.

section.name: Clarification
section.t: The SRH is processed per . One objective of that processing is to determine the value to place in the Destination Address field of the IPv6 packet. To this end, the next entry in the SID list in the SRH is processed and mapped to the value to place in the Destination Address field.
The value placed in the 128-bit Destination Address field of an IPv6 packet header needs to be a routable IPv6 address since that is required for forwarding the packet.

Note that entries in the SID list do not need to be fully formed IPv6 addresses that are copied directly to the Destination Address field of the IPv6 packet. The mapping from SID list entry to the destination address could be a direct copy (the SID list contains a list of IPv6 addresses) or could involve a more complex function.

An example of such a function is shown in , where a REPLACE-CSID compressed SID is expanded to be placed in the Destination Address field. Note that formally updates to allow this mapping function -- such an update would not have been needed if this document had already existed.

section.name: HMAC Processing in Section 2.1.2.1 of RFC 8754
section.t: In describing the Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) processing, the text in says that HMAC verification checks that the destination address of the packet matches that indicated by the next entry in the Segment List.

ul.li: HMAC Segments Left is less than or equal to Last Entry, and the destination address is equal to Segment List[Segments Left].

section.t: This is updated to allow a nondirect mapping from the Segment List entry to the destination address as follows:

ul.li: HMAC Segments Left is less than or equal to the Last Entry, and the destination address is equal to the address created by mapping from Segment List[Segments Left].

section.t: Further, in describing the concatenation of information to generate the text field input to the HMAC computation, says:

section.name: ICMP Processing in Section 5.4 of RFC 8754
section.t: The method for deriving the destination address of the invoking packet in reads as:

ul.li: The SID at Segment List[0] may be used as the destination address of the invoking packet.

section.t: To allow for the zeroth entry in the Segment List to be mapped rather than copied to a destination address, this is updated to:

ul.li: The SID at Segment List[0] may be mapped to derive the destination address of the invoking packet.

section.name: Operational Considerations
section.t: This document does not change any elements of the SRv6 architecture and, as such, it makes no change to the operational procedures or management tools of SR.

In clarifying the nature of SID list processing, this document also clarifies the nature of SID list entries. Operational and management tools that examine the SID list in a packet need to be aware of the nature of those entries in order to offer maximal clarity to the users of those tools.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This document makes no changes to the security properties of SRv6. See , , and for more discussion of SRv6 security.
Note that describing the SID list entries as being mapped to the destination address of a packet enables potential additional security mechanisms, such as encrypting the SID list.
